question.prompt: On a trip from the United States to Canada, Isabella took \(d\) U.S. dollars. At the border she exchanged them all, receiving \(10\) Canadian dollars for every \(7\) U.S. dollars. After spending \(60\) Canadian dollars, she had \(d\) Canadian dollars left. What is the sum of the digits of \(d?\)

solutions.explanation:
The exchange rate puts the numerical amounts before and after the exchange in the ratio \(7:10\). Represent the starting U.S. dollar amount by \(7\) equal parts and the received Canadian dollar amount by \(10\) equal parts.

The remaining Canadian dollar amount has the same numerical value \(d\) as the starting U.S. dollar amount, so it also corresponds to \(7\) parts. Therefore, the \(60\) Canadian dollars spent represent \(10-7=3\) parts. This determines the size of each part and then the starting amount:
\[
\text{one part}=60\div3=20,
\qquad d=7\cdot20=140.
\]
Checking the conditions, \(140\) U.S. dollars exchange for \(200\) Canadian dollars, leaving \(140\) after spending \(60\). Thus the requested digit sum is \(1+4+0=\boxed{5}\), choice \(\text{A}\).
solutions.title: Proportional parts
